title: The Glassmaker Who Invented Reading Glasses
event_summary: Salvino d'Armate, a Florentine glassmaker, is credited by a now-lost memorial plaque in the Church of Santa Maria Maggiore as the inventor of wearable eyeglasses around 1286. Working alongside Dominican friar Alessandro della Spina, who helped disseminate the technology, these artisans ground convex lenses into frames that could be perched on the nose, allowing aging scholars, monks, and merchants to continue reading and working past the age of 40. Within a decade, spectacle-making workshops spread across northern Italy and then throughout Europe, creating an entirely new artisan trade.
why_forgotten: The invention emerged from anonymous guild workshops where individual credit was rarely recorded, and d'Armate's memorial plaque was destroyed during church renovations in the 18th century. Historians have debated whether d'Armate was even real or a later fabrication, and the lack of a single dramatic moment—spectacles spread gradually through craft networks—made the story unsuitable for grand historical narratives. The technology was so quickly taken for granted that no one thought to celebrate its revolutionary origin.
why_it_matters: Eyeglasses effectively doubled the productive intellectual lifespan of every literate person in the world, arriving just in time to supercharge the Renaissance by allowing scholars, artists, and merchants to work well into old age. Without corrective lenses, Gutenberg's printing press would have had a dramatically smaller reading public, and the entire trajectory of mass literacy would have been delayed by generations. Today, over 4 billion people worldwide rely on corrective lenses, making this anonymous medieval invention arguably the most widely used technology in human history.
